Query voice: didactic coaching aimed at researchers/PhD students; explicit signposting (“The first habit… The second…” / “What is the equivalent…?”); sustained analogy (sports/chess -> research); first-person vignette + humility disclaimers; long multi-clause sentences with em-dashes/parentheticals; pragmatic/actionable framing about learning (social learning, deliberate practice), and a blog-post cadence.

All candidates here miss key fingerprints:
- Many are third-person science journalism (Quanta-style) with scene-setting, quotes, and narrative leads ([10043], [10866], [11219], [9705], [9775], [7623], [11188], [8076], [5840], [6268]) — not first-person coaching or structured advice.
- Several are technical documentation/release-note/tutorial prose ([4486], [11803], [8671]) — domain-specific, imperative but not reflective/analogical, no PhD/research-improvement theme.
- Several are AI safety/forecasting memo-posts with “Epistemic status/TL;DR” and factor lists ([11084], [9377], [3262], [6358], [11270], [9753], [3725], [2321]) — adjacent rationalist formatting, but they lack the sports-to-research analogy, the mentor/skill-building focus, and the particular conversational humility + pedagogical narrative flow of the query. They read more like research reports/position pieces than coaching advice.

Search cues for next hop: look for posts explicitly about ‘becoming a better researcher/PhD student’, ‘research taste’, ‘how to read papers’, ‘learning by imitation’, ‘watch experts work’, ‘office hours / asking questions’, ‘deliberate practice’ in research; expect numbered habits, section headers, rhetorical questions (“What’s the analog in X?”), and frequent em-dash/parenthetical clarifications plus modest self-positioning (“I’m not an expert, but…”).
hops.summary: No clear same-author matches in this hop. Candidates cluster into (1) science journalism, (2) technical docs/tutorials, and (3) AI-safety/rationalist essays; none reproduce the query’s first-person, analogy-driven, PhD-skill coaching style.

hops.search_query: "act-reflect-ask" research blog "film study" PhD students habit "What is the equivalent" "off-the-cuff" reactions
hops.notes:
Only [64] matches the query’s first-person, didactic coaching voice aimed at PhD/research skill. Shared fingerprints: (1) explicit signposting and framing questions (“Before we discuss… what does … even mean?”; “Here is my suggestion.”) similar to “The first habit… The second…” and “What is the equivalent…?”; (2) pragmatic definitions grounded in PhD-program norms (oral exam, papers, passing criteria) rather than abstract theorizing; (3) measured hedging + scope limits (“We could just dismiss… but…”, “for the most part… (yet)”, “I’ve not had luck…”) echoing the query’s humility disclaimers; (4) straightforward, conversational academic prose—short paragraphs, simple punctuation, occasional dash for qualification—without journalistic scene-setting. 

Most others are clear non-matches because they are (a) third-person science journalism with quotes, narrative leads, and reported speech ([2608], [10452], [3985], [9939], [8565], [8725], [10893], [3827], [6446], [8808], [2684], [8743], [9840], [10540])—missing first-person coaching and structured advice; (b) LW/EA/AI-safety essays with different signature formatting and aims (series headers, employer disclaimers, heavy argumentation about alignment/policy) ([8499], [8217], [2320], [4278])—they may have signposting/hedging but not the sports-to-research habit-building pedagogy; (c) highly technical tutorial/research-note style in ML/mechanistic interp or programming ([10573], [1887])—no PhD skill-building analogies, different cadence; (d) high-energy slang/diary voice ([4445])—tone and register don’t match; (e) [2107] is thematically adjacent (PhD/research development) but the style diverges: more sociological exposition + bullet-list manifesto, less conversational analogy-driven coaching and fewer rhetorical “analog/equivalent” moves.

Expect structured enumeration (first/second), rhetorical questions, and hedged claims rather than polished journalism or dense technical writeups.

hops.search_query: "But the datasheet doesn’t have enough information to tell you that; you just have to know" "chip hour" FLOPs 10^26 10^25 "times these numbers by 1.5"
hops.notes:
Query style: bloggy policy/compute-cost explainer with lots of inline numerics and back-of-the-envelope math; short declarative paragraphs; frequent em-dashes; rhetorical questions (“What is the difference…?” “Let’s say…”); explicit “Assumptions:” lists; unit-carrying calculations laid out stepwise; colloquial asides + insider detail footnote (“you just have to know!”); tech-specific proper nouns (H100/A100, FP8/BF16) and references to frontier labs; pragmatic tone aimed at practitioners/regulators.

None of the candidates match this combination. Many candidates are clearly Quanta-style magazine prose (4722, 11973, 7840, 7842, 7729, 11709, 10605, 4982): long narrative intros, quotes, scene-setting, attribution-heavy—missing the calculation walkthroughs and assumption blocks.

Some candidates are technical blog posts (1804 Rust pointers; 5499 consistency training) or EA/AI safety posts (5935, 8066, 4699, 6618, 2613, 10620), but their syntactic fingerprints differ: more essay/argument structure, fewer explicit unit calculations, different punctuation habits, and lack the distinctive ‘regulatory threshold + compute cost spreadsheet’ framing.

For next hop, look for texts with: explicit FLOP thresholds; GPU chip-hour costing; “Assumptions:” sections; step-by-step arithmetic with scientific notation; regulatory policy comparisons US vs EU; and casual footnote-y corrections about datasheets/specs.
hops.summary: No candidate snippet in this hop appears to be by the same author as the query. The closest topical neighborhood is AI safety/policy writing, but stylistic markers (assumption blocks + numeric cost derivations + colloquial spec footnotes) are absent.

hops.search_query: "I've tried to bring up arguments that would make people feel uncomfortable and defensive" "flow-through" effects "effective altruist movement" "tried and true" "default" options "earning to give"
hops.notes:
Query text signals an analytic-argumentative blog/essay style: explicit caveats and scope limits (“short and incomplete”), intentional discomforting tone, enumerated bullet points, frequent hedges (“it seems to me,” “I doubt,” “I do believe”), and a habit of defining what the author means by framing an implicit theme. Also notable: careful distinction between criticizing a movement vs. praising exemplars; use of quotation marks to distance/flag terms (“tried and true,” “earning to give”); and rhetorical questions (“Why do I call these things an ‘issue’?”).

Matches:
- [2963] shares the same legal-analytic argumentative cadence, sustained analogy-testing (“But does this analogy really hold?”), careful definitions, and measured normative language; similar paragraph structure with examples and hedges.
- [1822] matches on meta-level methodological argument, explicit rebuttal of an easy dismissal, tri-part bullet list of goals, and the same earnest, caveated, reader-addressing tone.
- [5727] matches on “I was thinking about X, ran into problem Y, here’s a writeup,” explicit uncertainty/novelty disclaimers, section headers, footnote markers, and step-by-step reasoning with illustrative examples.

Non-matches: Many other candidates are journalistic science writing (Quanta-style), transcripts, or highly idiosyncratic personal/sexual/meditation narrative; they lack the query’s EA-community critique posture, hedged normative argumentation, and structured point-by-point analytic rhetoric.
hops.summary: Found three strong stylistic matches (2963, 1822, 5727) characterized by structured critique, explicit caveats, hedged claims, rhetorical questions, and bullet/sectioned analytic exposition; most other candidates appear to be journalism, interviews/transcripts, or very different personal-narrative styles.

hops.search_query: "I've tried to bring up arguments that would make people feel uncomfortable and defensive" "effective altruist" critique "short and incomplete" "Lest this essay give a mistaken impression"
hops.notes:

The query is an EA-community critique written in a careful, argumentative blog-essay voice: explicit scope/limitations (“short and incomplete”), reader-management and caveats (“Lest this essay…”, “I should note…”), enumerated lists of grievances, hedging throughout (“it seems to me,” “I doubt,” “I do believe”), and metacommentary about what the essay is trying to do (make readers uncomfortable/defensive). It also uses frequent scare quotes to flag contested in-group terms (“tried and true,” “default,” “earning to give,” “flow-through”).

Most candidates are missing these fingerprints. hops.search_query: "Import A-Idea" "An occasional longer form essay series" OR ("pile of clothes on a chair" lampshade bookshelf "the room is our planet" AI) OR ("Technological Optimism and Appropriate Fear" "The Curve" conference Berkeley) OR ("fiendishly complex" "situational awareness" load-bearing "odd larping")
hops.notes:
QUERY authorial fingerprints: rhetorically vivid, story-first framing (child-in-the-dark parable), then pivots to policy/strategy claims; short emphatic paragraphs; heavy use of contrastive markers (“Now…”, “But make no mistake:”, “In fact,”); repeated concrete imagery (pile of clothes / bookshelf / lampshade) used as motif; confident moral/affective stance (“inherently very scary”) paired with analytic caveats (“not load-bearing”); conference-talk cadence (stage-setting time/place, audience-addressing “you”); preference for coined/labelled concepts and slogans.

Among candidates, [6367] matches strongly: geopolitical/AI strategy essay voice; introduces a coined term (“Jackpot Jinx”) and critiques another coined acronym (MAIM vs MAD); uses parenthetical clarification, game/strategy framing, and equilibrium language while maintaining punchy, persuasive rhetoric. Similar rhythm of setup → analogy critique → named concept → structured argument.

Non-matches: most other candidates are journalistic science features (Quanta-like), highly expository with reported quotes and third-person narration; or tutorial/how-to; or EA personal finance memo; or rationalist habit/TAP post—these lack the parable-style imagery, the ‘speech’ cadence, and the specific blend of emotive fear + policy prescription. Missing in non-matches: direct second-person admonitions, repeated motif imagery, and the author’s habit of explicitly declaring what is/isn’t “load-bearing” to their thesis.

For next hop: look for AI governance / national security / deterrence analogies, coined terms with catchy alliteration, speech/remarks formatting, parable openings, and emphatic signposting (“make no mistake”, “central challenge”, “your only chance”).
hops.summary: Only candidate [6367] appears to share the query author’s distinctive conference-remarks rhetorical style: vivid framing plus strategic-policy analysis with coined concepts and punchy signposting. Other candidates read like journalism or technical/blog exposition without the same voice.

Sentence structure is short-to-medium, crisp, with occasional nerd-jargon ("default policy", "stochastic", "conversion rate") applied to romance. 

None of the candidates match this distinctive satirical-microeconomics-of-dating style. Many candidates are straight science journalism, technical AI posts, or earnest essays with different cadence and rhetorical goals. What’s missing across candidates: invented-units-as-comedy, mock utilitarian accounting of romance, frequent definitional framing (Q&A format), and the specific mix of deadpan + lightweight self-aware caveats.

Closest *topic-adjacent* but still not a match: some rationalist-ish/technical posts (e.g., AI alignment/inference verification) share list structures and caveats, but lack the comedic unit-invention and dating-domain satire that are the core authorial fingerprint here.

[Hop 2]: Closest match is [8245]. It shares the query’s playful pseudo-technical/bloggy satire vibe: rapid-fire contemporary references, colloquial punchiness (“who dis?”), rhetorical micro-gags (“o3-mini-high which is somewhat less mini”), and a self-aware, slightly chaotic enumeration style (improvised acronyms, parenthetical naming attempts). What’s mostly MISSING from the rest: invented quantitative units applied to a non-technical domain; deadpan ‘definition + caveats/edge cases’ structure; mock-precision with discounting/negative values; footnote-like asides; and the specific rationalist/utilitarian accounting tone applied to romance. Most other candidates are straight science journalism (Quanta-like intros), academic/technical summaries, or earnest explanatory essays with a more formal cadence and fewer comedic pivots.

For next-hop searching, look for: posts that coin jokey measurement units or metrics, do faux-rigorous definitions with caveats, use parenthetical digressions and footnote markers, and end with a deadpan sincerity check (e.g., “I’m X% joking”). Also look for Q&A structures, ‘default policy’/decision-theory vocabulary used outside its normal domain, and humorous treatment of discount rates/expected value in everyday life.

It shares the query’s distinctive blend of (a) quantified pseudo-rigor (pace, kph, heart rate, time-to-effect), (b) casual, conversational first-person narration with abrupt comedic pivots, and (c) explicit meta-asides and punchlines (“Though I wish this was about moderating curse words…”, profanity used for rhythm/emphasis). The AI/rationalist posts ([2468], [10418], [4566], etc.) share analytical structure and some punchy aphorisms, but they read earnest, expansive, and externally focused (benchmarks, markets, energy economics) and lack the query’s core gimmick: invented units + deadpan definitional satire + romance/ordinary-life application. [7282] has casual humor (“multiple guys. You get it.”) and procedural structure, but not the mock-quantitative/decision-theory satirical framing.

To find more by this author next hop: search for first-person blog posts that combine numbers/metrics as a narrative device, snappy section headers, parenthetical jokes, and occasional deliberately over-precise quantification (heart rate, conversion rates, ‘X% joking’). Look for pieces that read like rationalist-adjacent life-hacking or self-experimentation with comedic deadpan, plus footnote-ish asides and edge-case caveats.

hops.search_query: "Enter structural risk minimization" "prior beliefs" "hypothesis class" "minimum description length" "agnostic PAC learnability"
hops.notes:
Query style: didactic/lecture-note voice about ML theory; heavy use of formal definitions (ε, δ), named frameworks (PAC, SRM, MDL), math inequality/sample complexity bounds, and rhetorical scaffolding (“Roughly…”, “In other words…”, “Now, how did we…?”, “One way to think about it is…”). The prose is explanatory with smooth transitions and a preference for building from definitions to implications to motivating questions; minimal narrative/scene-setting. Also has minor typos/formatting artifacts (duplicated words, broken LaTeX like m≥1ϵlog(|H|$δ), missing parentheses), suggesting informal notes copied from markdown/LaTeX.

None of the candidates match this exact authorial fingerprint. Closest thematically are technical ML/AI posts ([11119], [2197], [8698]) but they have distinctive markers not present in the query: strong first-person lab-notebook voice (“I tried…”, “I found…”, “plot twist”), explicit program/course boilerplate (“Epistemic status”, “created as part of…”), TLDR headers, and more informal startup/blog cadence. The long science-journalism excerpts ([2548], [5810], [8119], etc.) are clearly different: narrative reporting, quotes, and polished magazine style. The query lacks TLDR/epistemic-status tropes and lacks personal narrative, which rules out most LessWrong/EA-style candidates in this batch.

For next hop: look for texts that (a) teach ML theory in a neutral textbook tone, (b) use PAC/VC/generalization bounds/MDL/SRM vocabulary, (c) include inline math and “Roughly / In other words / Now…” transition questions, and (d) show light markdown/LaTeX conversion glitches rather than polished typesetting.
hops.summary: No candidate text in this set appears to be by the same author as the query; candidates split into science journalism and first-person AI/EA blog posts with different structural and stylistic conventions.

hops.search_query: "Lessons from a Dropped Ball" convolution "In a previous post" "frontier of convolutional neural networks" "Thankfully, with a few examples"
hops.notes:
QUERY style: didactic technical blog/tutorial voice; first-person plural (“we”) guiding the reader; frequent rhetorical questions (“How likely is it…?” “Let’s break this down.”); step-by-step construction of an example; heavy use of inline math notation with named variables (a,b,c), distributions f(a), g(b), and a summation ∑a+b=c; emphasis on intuition before formalism (“without referring to any significant mathematics…”, “Thankfully, with a few examples…”). Paragraphs are short and scaffolded; uses colon to introduce formulas; uses ellipses to indicate omitted terms; occasional footnote marker “.1”.

MISSING from all candidates: this particular combination of (1) gentle pedagogy aimed at building intuition for a core math concept, (2) tight integration of probability-example narrative with explicit symbolic derivation, and (3) the exact cadence markers (“Let’s…”, “Imagine…”, “Thankfully…”) plus the minimalist variable naming (a,b,c) and explicit convolution-style constraint a+b=c.

Why top-scoring candidates don’t match: many are journalistic science writing (Quanta-like) with quoted experts, historical narrative, and no first-person tutorial derivation; several are policy/AI-safety commentary with long legal/empirical summaries; some are ML theory posts but in a different register (bullet lists, programmatic definitions, alignment jargon, less story-driven probability vignette). None show the same ‘intro intuition → discrete example → sum over partitions → compact sigma notation’ teaching pattern.
hops.summary: No candidate text in hop 1 strongly matches the query author’s distinctive pedagogical, math-derivation tutorial style for explaining convolution via a probability story; candidates cluster into science journalism, policy analysis, or different-form ML theory writing.

Mixes concrete visual details with a moral/psychological interpretation, and drops a specific scholar citation + bullet list.

None of the candidates match this fingerprint. Most are either: (a) formal technical essays with numbered sections, definitions, hedging, and long expository sentences (AI alignment, logic, infra-Bayes), (b) magazine-style science journalism with reported speech and neutral tone (Quanta-like), or (c) personal memoir/learning narrative without the art/perspective puzzle structure and distinctive emphatic punctuation.

Missing from candidates relative to query: the second-person guided-looking-at-an-image mode; the sharp pivot from confusion to insight; heavy use of exclamation points/ellipses for excitement; interpretive art-historical moral framing; and the specific 'reconstruction solves an apparent paradox' storytelling pattern.

The query has: (1) a personal conversion arc (“never appealed… but now I realize”), (2) direct second-person staging (“You’re staring…”), (3) short punchy paragraphs and rhetorical questions, (4) conspicuous excitement markers (multiple exclamation points, ellipses, interjections like “Astounding!”, “whoosh”), (5) a paradox/puzzle setup resolved by a specific scholarly reconstruction + diagram, (6) concrete visual inventory (oranges, Bass ale, green shoes) plus moral/psychological interpretation, and (7) informal-but-informed art-history context dropped midstream.

hops.search_query: "Feel free to bring this up in five years" Redshift Snowflake "folk wisdom" "lowest layer" cloud vendors

hops.notes:
Matches: all three have a distinctly bloggy, first-person engineering-nerd voice that mixes informal evaluation with concrete examples. Frequent short paragraphs, “here’s the problem / here’s what I tried” sequencing, and a preference for showing artifacts (tables, generated n-grams, numbered lists) as rhetorical evidence. They use casual intensifiers and judgment (“comically dumb”, “pretty weird”, “mostly noise”, “absolutely batshit insane”), and they do the anticipatory-argument pattern (state an intuition, then undercut it with why it fails). Also similar is the habit of enumerating issues as a list of bullets/numbered points and using parenthetical asides.

Non-matches: many others are either (a) Quanta-style magazine journalism with quotes and polished scene-setting ([6060], [5546], [10381], [6406], [7460], [8178]) or (b) LessWrong/EA ‘epistemic status’ / alignment discourse with heavy abstraction and meta-caveats ([6520], [10730], [6449], [11523], [8497], [9056], [3823], [9913], [2349], [4280]) or (c) straight tutorial/code voice without the ranty contrarian cadence ([2168]) or (d) more academic methodology prose ([11696]). What’s missing in most non-matches relative to the query author: developer-tooling contrarianism, hyperbolic quantities (“trillion”), snarky dismissals, and the punchy manifesto-like prescriptions.

Extra fingerprints to seek next hop: strong reliance on lists/tables as ‘proof’, blunt value-judgments embedded in technical exposition, rhetorical pivots like “Ok, so…”, “To give you an idea…”, “Of course…”, and a tendency to call out why naive approaches are ‘noise’ or ‘dumb’ then propose a pragmatic alternative. Topic adjacency likely: search/indexing, data/analysis, systems/dev tooling critiques, contrarian takes on tech decisions.
hops.summary: Found three plausible same-author matches: [787] (search/index query rewriting writeup with the same informal diagnostic cadence), [549] (TF‑IDF on Linux commit messages with similar ‘this is noise / of course… / ok so’ voice and tables), and [11683] (ranty critique of a sci‑fi premise using the same blunt, list-driven argument style). Most other candidates diverge into journalism, alignment/EA epistemic-status prose, or pure tutorial/academic tones.

Shared vocabulary/tics: “script”, “box”, “pretty”, “spectacularly”, “comically dumb”, “to give you an idea…”.

Likely NOT same author: most other candidates are either formal expository/academic (969, 6577), journalistic science writing (5514, 4112, 4948, 10110), or modern AI-safety/Substack rationalist style with headers/TL;DR/epistemic-status tropes (4963, 2968, 6679, 3779, 8422, 11529, 3678). Candidate 1778 has aphoristic parallel-structure (“Good Programmers are…”) and a moralizing tone, lacking the detailed system-integration narrative and gritty implementation specifics seen in QUERY.

[Hop 2]: Strong shared-author signals: conversational first-person sysadmin/engineering blog voice; rhetorical questions used to frame the topic (“Do you know why…?”, “What kind of things…?”); short punchy paragraphs; pragmatic, gritty infrastructure focus (process lists, sockets, privileges; ptrace, termios, controlling tty); casual intensifiers (“pretty”, “much, much better”); occasional profanity/edgier aside (“you’re screwed”, “give a shit”); habit of walking through how something works with concrete mechanisms and named tools/APIs; mild snark about real-world messiness; uses scare quotes and italics-like emphasis via capitalization (“Just Work”).

Patterns to seek next hop: Unix/Linux internals posts, tools/utilities announcements, deep-dives with a “How does it work?” section, lists of practical checks, and opinionated security/ops commentary. Likely missing from the author: academic/journalistic tone, long formal introductions, heavy citation/quote-driven narrative, polished magazine-style ledes, or overt rationalist/Substack header tropes.

Why others don’t match: many candidates are Quanta-like science journalism (third-person, quotation-heavy, explanatory lede); others are EA/rationalist/AI-safety essay styles with abstract framing and institutional tone; several are memoir/personal-psych prose. 1767 is first-person engineering but reads like retrospective anecdote inside a corporate history (less punchy/snarky, no checklist/pipeline vibe, different pacing).

Prefers gritty operational details over abstraction; uses mild snark/humor and rhetorical framing (“It goes like this:”, “Back to our cron job.”). Also matches the QUERY’s habit of enumerating moving parts and emphasizing messy glue logic rather than presenting a polished architecture.

549 matches the same ‘I poked at data with a quick script’ persona: first-person curiosity, quick-and-dirty analysis, tables, and a didactic progression (“Alright…”, “Ok, so…”, “Luckily…”). Match signals in [327]: first-person reflective tech-blog voice; explicit expectation-setting and epistemic updating ("Going in… I still expected…" / "my expectations were… out of date" / "thoughts are still unfolding"); pragmatic process write-up framed as "this piece is an attempt to…"; concrete quantitative specifics ("factor of 1000"; "from 90s to about 15ms"); lots of parenthetical asides and em-dash contrast; calm competence-signaling tone; operational tooling details (Emacs/Obsidian/Slack-adjacent) and an execution/playbook vibe (plan → constraints → approach). 

Non-matches: Most other candidates are third-person magazine-style science writing with quotes and scene-setting ([3605], [7328], [7099], [3263], [2755], [9561], [10252], [2689])—wrong POV and cadence. Several first-person rationalist/AI-risk essays ([10676], [3697], [3020], [8605]) share some analytic/hedging habits but lack the org-execution/project-management focus and have different rhythm (more thesis-y, less operational diary/playbook). [342] is first-person career anecdote but is more sentimental/thank-you narrative, with fewer hedging/nuance parentheses and less of the "here’s the playbook / here’s what I did" procedural structure. [1106] is first-person explanatory and structured, but its voice is more didactic/sectioned and the personal-org PM fingerprints (prioritization, trust, decisionmakers, false economy, autopilot) are not present; it also has distinctive stylistic quirks (numbered sections, heavier tutorial tone).

What to seek next hop: more first-person ops/engineering posts that (a) open with a belief-update or "I didn’t realize X"; (b) include concrete metrics and toolchain specifics; (c) use frequent parentheses/em-dashes for qualification; (d) emphasize execution mechanics (status-checking, coordination, prioritization) over ideology; (e) downplay impressiveness while highlighting straightforward high-leverage routines.
hops.summary: Only [327] strongly matches the query author’s first-person, hedged, operational playbook style with quantified specifics and parenthetical nuance. The rest are primarily third-person science journalism or first-person essays with a different (more polemical/didactic or anecdotal) cadence.

hops.search_query: "proper scoring rule" "Brier score" "oracle tells" "best bet" "This is not true for absolute error"
hops.notes:
Query text has a very distinctive didactic-mathy StackExchange/blog vibe: first-person motivation (“someone recently asked… so I decided…”), then a crisp thesis (“absolute error might match what you care about… however…”), followed by a structured list of mathematically framed bullet points with equations, invariance/parameterization arguments, and proper-scoring-rule discussion including a worked numeric counterexample. None of the candidates match that combination of (a) conversational SE-origin framing, (b) dense equation-heavy exposition, (c) repeated ‘On the other hand…’ contrasts, (d) invariance/coordinate-change language, and (e) explicit expected-score calculation in-line.

Many candidates are clearly journalistic longform (Quanta/Atlantic-style with quotes, scene-setting, named sources) or LessWrong/EA organizational/advocacy posts (headers, TL;DR, governance, hiring, alignment proposals) or hobbyist lists/reviews. A few are math-adjacent explainers (e.g., eigenvectors/tensors/PCP) but read like edited popular science reporting rather than a personal-answer adaptation; they lack the query’s personal SE prompt, list-of-properties proof-sketch cadence, and equation-centric argumentation. Also missing across candidates: the exact punctuation/format habits in the query (LaTeX-y inline symbols, vector notation, explicit estimator/minimizer claims, invariance claims), and the particular rhetorical move of ‘you might think X matters practically, but Y wins for mathematical reasons’ with multiple independent examples.
hops.summary: No candidate text in this hop appears to be by the same author as the query. The closest topical matches are popular-science math explainers, but their journalistic tone/structure and lack of SE-style equation-driven argumentation make common authorship unlikely.

[Hop 1]: Query authorial fingerprints: conversational-yet-analytical blog voice; lots of em-dashes, parentheses for asides, and self-referential footnote-style markers (e.g., “software engineering.1”, “data preparation,2,” “prompt engineering3”); rhetorical contrast framing (“Traditional ML … Today … With LLMs, in contrast …”); mild snark (“snake oil”, “by hook or by crook”), HCI/UX framing, and long sentences built from clause chaining.

[626] matches the same “one of the X things” opener, short punchy paragraphs, casual tech/business register (“random dev”, “low pressure”, “market Intel”), playful quantified aside (“10 years LLM experience … my 20 conversations :)”), and similar pragmatic reflective tone.

What’s missing in non-matches: journalistic science feature cadence with quotes and scene-setting (e.g., Quanta/NYT-style intros), formal technical exposition (math/CS notation-heavy), or overt polemic/financial ranting. Also missing in most candidates: the distinctive footnote-number habit and the ML-workflow/HCI framing; [626] doesn’t have footnotes but otherwise aligns strongly on voice and structure.

[Hop 2]: Closest match is [6737]. It shares the same conversational-yet-analytical essay voice with lots of hedging and positioning (“Some historical context…”, “I would guess…”, “Unfortunately, probably not…”), long clause-chained sentences, and a habit of explaining a domain via workflow/friction/culture framing (here: why bio startups are hard; in query: why traditional ML is hard). It also uses casual emphasis and mild snark (“it really, really sucks”, “love of the game”) plus tech/biz product sensibility. Paragraphing cadence is similar: broad claim → personal/contextual aside → zoom into a concrete example.

What’s MISSING even in [6737]: the very distinctive footnote-number ticks (e.g., “software engineering.1”, “data preparation,2,”) and the heavy use of em-dashes/parenthetical asides is somewhat lower, though still present. Most other candidates fail due to being (a) formal tutorial/benchmark-y exposition [165], (b) journalistic quoted-scene science writing with named sources [8414, 4505, 9049, 3845, 4987, 6063, 4761, 9561, 11970], (c) LessWrong “Epistemic Status” / rationalist house-style with elaborate hypotheticals [3837, 2307, 3854, 11848, 5210, 7049, 10406], or (d) kernel dev documentation voice [10050]. For next hop, look for first-person ML/AI/product essays with HCI/UX/process framing, mild irreverence (“snake oil” vibe), contrast-structured sections (“Traditional… Today… With X…”), and ideally quirky inline footnote numerals.

[Hop 3]: Strong match on blog-essay voice: conversational-but-analytical with sharp contrast framing and self-aware stance-setting (“Let me be clear…”), long clause-chained sentences, and frequent parenthetical asides. Shares the same mild snark/irreverence and metaphor choices (“snake oil”, “bag of goods”, “palatable for clicks”), plus the same sociotechnical/industry-critique theme (AI hype, institutions, deployment consequences). Also matches the distinctive footnote-marker habit with inline numerals immediately after punctuation (“here.1”, “thing.2”), mirroring query (“software engineering.1”, “data preparation,2,”). Punctuation cadence aligns: em-dashes, rhetorical questions, short punchy paragraphs interleaved with long explanatory ones. What’s missing in non-matches: Quanta/journalistic scene-setting with quotes; formal math notation / tutorial structure; LessWrong-style ‘Epistemic status’ header; transcript/dialogue formatting.

[Hop 4]: None of the hop-4 candidates match the query author strongly enough to attribute to the same person.

Key query-author fingerprints to look for (and mostly missing here):
- Conversational-but-analytical ML/LLM workflow commentary with HCI/UX framing (progress indicators, sunk cost, org incentives) rather than straight news, pure technical writeups, or politics.
- Heavy use of clause-chained long sentences + frequent parenthetical asides and em-dash interruptions, with mild snark (“snake oil”, “by hook or by crook”).
- Distinctive inline footnote-number markers attached to punctuation/words (e.g., “software engineering.1”, “data preparation,2,” “prompt engineering3”). None of these candidates show that exact tick.
- Structural contrast signposting (“Traditional ML… Today… With LLMs, in contrast…”) and rhetorical questions; several candidates are listy/Table-of-Contents roundups or magazine-style expository intros.

Closest-but-not-same:
- [2940], [10847], [4280], [2736] have a bloggy, opinionated cadence, snark, and TOC/list habits typical of certain AI roundup writers, but they lack the HCI/UX ML-lifecycle angle and (critically) the footnote-marker quirk; their voice is more “weekly roundup / newsletter” with lots of headers.
- [6328] is technical-engineering documentation style (benchmarks, architecture overview), not the reflective sociotechnical essay voice.
- [5384] is reported-politics Substack voice with sourcing and updates.
- [9684], [10650], [5512], [8849], [11929], [7328], [11219] are Quanta-like magazine science features with scene-setting, quotes, and explanatory narration—clearly different authorial house style.
- [7307], [9608], [4370], [4241], [4348], [10249], [5203], [7035], [11836] are rationalist/EA or personal-experiment posts with different tics (e.g., explicit “Epistemic status”, TL;DR blocks, bullet-heavy structure) and without the query’s specific footnote-number habit.

What to search for next hop:
- First-person essays explicitly about ML engineering/LLM product building friction, evaluation, monitoring, deployment expectations.
- Posts with quirky inline footnote numerals (not bracketed citations) and lots of parenthetical asides/em-dashes.
- Language mixing ML ops details with UX/HCI framing and org-psych commentary (sunk cost, leadership misunderstanding, hype cycles).

hops.search_query: "coarse-grained lineage" mltrace "entrepreneur-in-residence" "Amplify Partners" "production ML pipelines" "trace a prediction" "most upstream"
hops.notes:
Query text has a first-person, builder/entrepreneur voice; tight technical-product framing; lots of ML/MLOps jargon used pragmatically (pipeline, production, lineage, tracing); skimmable structure with headings (“What I’m working on”, “Why…”), short paragraphs, and indented/bulleted roadmaps with parenthetical examples like “(ex: …)”. What’s missing in candidates: (1) product-announcement cadence (dev release/demo/roadmap), (2) explicit MLOps/production ML pipeline domain vocabulary, (3) the ‘I’m building X tooling I wish I had’ founder tone, (4) concise, action-oriented engineering prose.

Most candidates are either long-form magazine journalism (Quanta-style third-person reported narratives with quotes, scene-setting, dates, proper nouns) or essayist/rationalist takes on AGI/society with different rhythms and concerns. Even the technical RL paper excerpt is formal academic style, not founder/blog announcement style.
hops.summary: No candidate text in this hop appears to be written by the same author as the query; styles cluster into science journalism, academic writing, or AGI-focused personal essays rather than a concise MLOps tooling announcement with roadmap bullets.

hops.search_query: "entrepreneur-in-residence" "Amplify Partners" "open-source" (mltrace OR "lineage" OR tracing) "production ML" pipelines roadmap "dev release" "I wish I had"
hops.notes:
Best match: [1061] shares the same “builder-researcher” voice: first-person agenda-setting (“I’m interested in…”, “Concretely, suppose…”), pragmatic ML engineering vocabulary (compute, checkpoints, pretraining runs), and skimmable structure with section headers + enumerated/stepwise experimental suggestions. It also uses the same rhetorical pattern of defining a concept, then immediately operationalizing it into concrete experiments and plots.

Partial-but-not-same: [7448] has announcement energy (“We are excited to announce…”, mission/goals bullets) but is institution/program marketing with heavy proper-noun/location logistics; lacks the founder ‘tooling I’m building’ + production pipeline/ops focus and has a more organizational ‘we’ voice.

Clear non-matches: Quanta-style journalism excerpts ([8350],[10122],[6642],[6110],[2689],[10794],[10863],[8468],[8287],[9326]) are third-person narrative with quotes/scene-setting; not the concise product/research memo style. Rationalist/personal-health posts ([9153],[9809],[11683]) have edgy anecdotal tone and long narrative digressions unlike the crisp technical product framing. Formal/aphoristic math essay ([11640]) is rhetorically ornate and abstract. Interpretability note ([4906]) is closer in topic but has a different cadence (long paragraphy, footnote-heavy, less ‘shipping/roadmap’ framing). [987] is first-person workflow blogging and structured steps, but it’s about writing/LLMs and reads more like creator-economy/process advice than infra/product for production pipelines; still could be adjacent but stylistically it’s more polished/SEO and less domain-specific.

Authorial fingerprints to use next hop: first-person ‘I’m building/working on X’, product/research announcement cadence (release/demo/roadmap), emphasis on productionization/ops, bullet-roadmap items with parenthetical examples “(ex: …)”, mild anti-buzzword caveats, and immediate grounding into concrete engineering tasks (trace output back to raw file; rerun stale components; monitoring integrations).
hops.summary: Only candidate [1061] plausibly matches the query author’s first-person technical agenda + concrete-experiment/engineering memo style. Others diverge into journalism, institutional announcements, personal essays, or abstract math.

hops.search_query: "AI Savior" saviorism applied machine learning "Gartner hype cycle" "project fairs" Stanford undergrad "deep learning for genomics"
hops.notes: Query text has a distinctive first-person reflective/critical essay style about ML culture: moral-historical framing (explicitly citing Kipling/“White Man’s Burden”), coined label (“AI Saviors”), careful hedging + norms signaling (avoids calling out individuals), and structured intent bullets (“In light of this worrying trend, I want to: …”). Sentence rhythm mixes academic exposition with conversational asides; uses em dashes and quotation marks for scare quotes; references personal Stanford experience and course-project dynamics. None of the candidates match this combination. Many candidates are (a) Quanta-style third-person science journalism (2474/11906/4371/5596/10122/10008/3126/3980/4917/11960), (b) LW/EA ‘epistemic status’ research posts with TL;DR headers and technical benchmarking tone (9306/7618/8816/7290/11887/11886/8707/3823), or (c) contrarian medical/biohacking critiques (10051/7558) with different cadence and ideology. Missing from candidates: the postcolonial/imperialism analogy, the “saviorism” framing applied to ML, the autobiographical Stanford undergrad narrative, and the explicit meta-ethical ‘not naming names’ stance.
hops.summary: No clear same-author matches in this hop; candidates cluster into science journalism and LW/EA-style technical posts, which do not share the query’s autobiographical, culturally critical ‘AI saviorism’ essay voice.

hops.search_query: "The bike messenger was the perfect myth" authenticity totemic value vestigial interest in fixies "In this era of ubiquitous information"
hops.notes:
QUERY voice: first-person memoir + cultural critique; short punchy paragraphs; rhetorical questions; ironic/knowing tone; advertising/tech-labor authenticity theme; casual but precise vocabulary; occasional italicized/Capitalized emphasis (e.g., “Authentic”); parenthetical asides and specific brand-name examples; sentence fragments used for rhythm.

MATCH: [8751] shares the same authorial fingerprints: conversational internet-aware opener (“If you ask the internet…”), emphatic caps for quoted social-pressure slogans, numbered list of mechanisms, skeptical empiricism framed in plain language, and a distinctive jokey analogy (“Babies that wear baby Rolex watches…”). It also uses rhetorical pivots (“But if you look for evidence…”) and casual punctuation with parentheses.

MISMATCHES: The Quanta Magazine-style science journalism pieces ([10650], [6359], [8580], [7461], etc.) are third-person reported narratives with lots of attribution quotes and formal exposition—missing the personal-ad-industry reminiscence, irony, and internet-culture rhetorical moves. For next hop: look for essays with (1) internet-skeptical, evidence-oriented contrarian takes, (2) playful analogies, (3) lots of parenthetical asides, (4) list-based breakdowns, (5) rhetorical questions, and (6) cultural critique of institutions/industries framed through personal experience.
hops.summary: Only candidate [8751] strongly matches the query’s conversational, irony-tinged cultural-critique style with emphatic typography, list structures, and playful analogies; the rest are predominantly formal science journalism or technical/rationalist exposition with different narrative stance and cadence.

hops.search_query: "human input" "useful AI output" ratio "mythical" AGI timelines "jumping-off point" "carrying capacity"
hops.notes:
Query style: essayistic, first-person analytical voice; frames a popular discourse (“AGI timelines”) then critiques underlying assumptions; uses contrast pairs (“long” vs “short”), rhetorical questions, and proposes an alternate metric (“ratio of human input per useful AI output”). Characteristic: clear, compact paragraphs; conversational but precise; mild hedging (“may be possible”), no heavy citations; emphasis on measurement/curves/trends and economic framing.

All candidates here mismatch strongly. Many are journalistic science features (Quanta-like) with scene-setting, quotes, third-person narration, and section headers ([4617], [2474], [2576], [10794], [7158], [3845], [8879], [3648]). Others are transcripts ([10921]) or job posting ([4736]) or technical PL theory exposition ([1823]) or git how-to ([2164])—different register and structure. The few bloggy/first-person pieces ([2663], [6927], [5737], [6299], [11222], [11263], [9366], [2441], [8958]) still diverge: they’re either literary/reflective, heavily citation-auditing, long-form with many asides/footnotes, or use distinct profanity/intimacy or different thematic focus. Missing from candidates: the specific ‘popular AGI timeline discourse → propose productivity-per-human-input metric’ argumentative arc, the crisp economic-measurement framing, and the particular balance of conversational tone + lightweight formalism.

For next hop, look for: short-to-medium rationalist/tech-essay posts that (1) open by referencing a trendy AI meme, (2) argue the meme implies hidden assumptions, (3) replace it with an operationalizable metric, often invoking curves/ratios and “per unit” productivity language, and (4) use rhetorical questions to pivot to measurement proposals; minimal quoting/interviewing; few/no external citations; contemporary AI policy/forecasting vibe.
hops.summary: No candidate text in this hop appears to share authorship with the query; candidates are predominantly journalistic science writing, transcripts, technical docs, or stylistically distinct blog posts.

[Hop 1]: QUERY fingerprint: first-person operator/founder voice; short punchy paragraphs; strong declaratives + contrarian reframes (“Operating well is a state, not an outcome”); heavy use of em dashes/hyphens for asides (“doesn’t mean… - it’s…”); rhetorical repetition/parallelism (“The first order effect… But the second order effect…”); section headers + list structure; direct imperatives (“Reinforce… Ask… Put…”); startup/product anecdotes with concrete examples (Stripe, feature cuts, timeframe); informal but sharp, coaching tone.

Match: [1042] shares the same founder-operator register, the same cadence (short lines, repeated “But…” pivots), the same hyphen-as-em-dash habit, and the same confident-but-humble stance (“There is no framework… I can’t offer…”). It also uses the same rhetorical pattern of setting up a common belief then flipping it.

Non-matches: Most other candidates are journalistic science writing (Quanta-style) with quotations, third-person narration, and long expository sentences; or technical ML/EA posts with “Epistemic status,” citations, and dense jargon; or other blog voices that don’t use the same imperative playbook framing and startup-operator anecdotal specificity. Several have list bullets but lack the Stripe/operator coaching tone and the distinctive ‘first/second order effects’ managerial framing.

What’s missing in non-matches: the operator/playbook vibe, the repeated goal/strategy/focus managerial motif, the crisp aphorisms, and the concrete product execution anecdote style.

[Hop 2]: No candidates strongly match the query’s founder/operator “operating manual” voice. The query has: (1) first-person operator credibility markers (Stripe, launching a product, timelines), (2) crisp aphorisms + contrarian reframes (“X is a state, not an outcome”), (3) tight coaching imperatives and playbook structure (section header → bullets → commands), (4) frequent pivot structure with “But…” and explicit “first-order/second-order effects” managerial framing, (5) hyphen-as-em-dash asides, and (6) concrete execution examples with feature lists and tradeoffs.

Most candidates here are missing those fingerprints: they’re either (a) third-person journalistic science/math profiles with quotes and long expository narration ([4056], [11242], [7629], [2851], [3195]), (b) technical research/blog posts with formal structure, citations, figures, and domain jargon (mechanistic interp, SDF, sequent calculus, natural latents, bpftrace) rather than operator coaching ([10668], [5938], [6151], [9281], [6266], [7930], [10597]), or (c) rationalist/EA conversational posts with “epistemic status”-adjacent hedging, meta, or experimental writeups—still not operator/playbook and lacking product/people management cadence ([7207], [7558], [4269], [11016], [11966], [3145]).

Patterns to look for next hop: short punchy declaratives; explicit management concepts (goals, focus, metrics, iteration, second-order effects); imperative checklist/bullets; operator anecdotes with concrete shipped-product details (feature cuts, timelines, adoption); confident coaching tone with humility beats; heavy use of dashes for parenthetical pivots; section headers like “Strategy & focus.”

[Hop 3]: Best match: [1848]. It shares the operator/industry-coaching register and “thought-leader” cadence: declarative reframes (“Good developer experience is not so much about… as it’s about…”), heavy contrast/pivot structure (“While it’s true…, it turns out…”; “But because…”; “So where do we go from here?”), and repeated em-dash interruptions used as parenthetical asides. It also uses section-like rhetorical framing and audience-addressing questions, plus generalized principles backed by concrete industry observations (developer tools, stacks, coordination), similar to the query’s goal/strategy/focus playbook tone.

Non-matches: most others are (a) third-person journalistic science/math writing with quotes, narrative exposition, and long explanatory paragraphs ([11785], [8113], [3263], [2689], [7328], [10580], [5617]); (b) technical/academic AI safety or math posts with formal definitions, citations, “Abstract”, and paper-like structure ([2928], [4819], [8714], [5935], [5474], [11409], [10742]); (c) personal essay/diary voice ([3684], [5979]); or (d) data/science analysis/blogging with a different persona and less operator-management imperative framing ([8062], [3816], [5410], [5051], [8605], [5753], [8789], [9792]).

Fingerprints to use next hop: first-person or collective-industry voice aimed at practitioners; crisp aphorisms/contrarian reframes (“X is a state, not an outcome”; “Focus is not about…”); frequent “But…” pivots and first/second-order framing; imperatives/checklists; em-dash asides; startup/product execution anecdotes (timelines, tradeoffs, feature cuts); section headers like “Strategy & focus.” What’s missing in most candidates is the operator playbook structure + concrete product execution story + managerial concepts (goals, focus, metrics, iteration) presented as advice.

[Hop 4]: No candidate cleanly matches the query’s founder/operator playbook voice. The query’s key fingerprints are: crisp aphoristic reframes (“X is a state, not an outcome”), imperative coaching bullets under a section header (“Strategy & focus.” → ‘Reinforce… Focus…’), repeated contrast pivots with “But…”, explicit managerial systems framing (“first order / second order effect”, goals→metrics→tactics), and a concrete product-execution anecdote with a feature-cut list and a named company/timebox (Stripe, “Payment Links”, “<6 months”, enumerated cut features). hops.search_query: "newly fallen constraint" bandwidth "forking of applications" developed markets developing markets smartphone OEMs move far faster than network infrastructure operators
hops.notes:
Query text reads like a tech/product essay (blog/newsletter) with a clear argumentative arc, short punchy paragraphs, lots of constraint/framing language (“memory constrained, CPU constrained…”, “newly missing constraint”), concrete consumer-app examples (Snapchat/Spotify/Gixo), and a market-structure conclusion (developed vs developing markets). Distinctive fingerprints: (1) repeated rhetorical pattern ‘The challenge for X is…’ / ‘This means…’; (2) contrastive historical framing (first generation vs next generation); (3) casual-but-precise tone, minimal citations, no quotes/interviews; (4) emphasis on product compromises, platform targets, infrastructure vs OEM replacement cycles.

All candidates here strongly mismatch: many are Quanta-style reported features with scene-setting intros, quotations, named sources, and journalistic narrative ([3120],[4412],[5333],[8081],[10561],[11876],[7210],[5969],[2458],[5596],[11322]); several are alignment-forum/technical research posts with heavy citations, acknowledgements, datasets, or formal sectioning ([4116],[8746],[7297],[7776],[9077]); others are org updates/annual reports with first-person admin/logistics focus ([9366],[9792]) or a different polemical voice ([9151]). What’s missing across candidates relative to the query: the tight ‘constraints enable products’ product-thinking lens, the consumer mobile/app examples, and the crisp infrastructure adoption argument without interviews/citations.

hops.notes:
QUERY STYLE: mathematically formal, blog-post voice with explicit agenda-setting (“Let me first address…”, “Having disposed of…”), sharp evaluative adjectives (“nonsense”, “harmful”, “lousy”), heavy use of logical metalanguage (object-language vs meta-language), symbols/notation (Boolean algebra/Heyting algebra, interpretation function, Lindenbaum–Tarski algebra), numbered enumerations of cases, and tight argumentative progression with occasional snark.

MISMATCHES IN CANDIDATES: Most candidates are journalism/transcripts (Quanta-style intros, interviews) with narrative leads, quotations, and lay exposition; or LW/EA-style AI-risk posts with “epistemic status”, bullets, and social/community framing; or personal habit/mental-health essays. None show the distinctive combination of (i) dense formal semantics/model-theory framing, (ii) insistence on syntactic well-formedness vs “syntactic garbage”, (iii) aggressive dismissal via logic laws, and (iv) algebraic semantics talk (Boolean/Heyting, interpretation function i: Sent→B, Lindenbaum–Tarski) in the same register.

WHAT TO LOOK FOR NEXT HOP: technical philosophy-of-logic / foundations blog posts; frequent LaTeX; discussion of semantics vs proof theory; talk of Boolean/Heyting algebras, models, interpretations, quotienting, Lindenbaum–Tarski; rhetorical structure: ‘two bad explanations’ then ‘three precise readings’; blunt corrective tone; phrases like “this is nonsense/meaningless”, “return to the drawing board”, “do not confuse meta- with object-…”.

hops.summary: No candidate strongly matches the query author’s consultative enterprise-software essay style (hype skepticism + migration realism + structured sections + parallel ‘Accepting…’ bullets). Query style markers: first-person, reflective self-critique; explicit probability/credence statements ("over 80%"); "model"/"reference class" language; careful quantitative comparisons; lots of hedging + epistemic humility ("I think", "likely", "I don't think so"); long paragraph chains with causal explanation; pragmatic, bloggy tone; uses parentheticals and asides; straightforward punctuation, minimal flourish.

Matches:
- [4825]: first-person empirical blog post; detailed experimental setup; quantitative framing; pragmatic explanations + asides ("spoilers"); similar sentence rhythm and "here’s what I did / what I found" structure.
- [7282]: instructive, pragmatic meetup writeup; casual rationalist-community vibe ("80/20"), direct imperatives, parenthetical notes/footnote markers; similar plainspoken tone.
- [5675]: list-format explanatory post; "please comment"; historical/nuclear reference-class vibe; simple declarative sentences, evidence-heavy.
- [8925]: first-person motivation; enumerated research questions; cautious framing; alignment/CoT transparency theme consistent with rationalist/AI-safety blogger voice.
- [11464]: first-person opinionated-but-analytic review; numbered dichotomy critique + proposing a “3rd way”; definition-by-breaking-terms-down ("Let’s break it down."); political/AI-safety policy focus consistent.

- Technical RL causal inference explainer [2054] is first-person but reads like a didactic ML blog with formal causal-diagram exposition and punchier subheads; less of the reflective, historically-comparative, credence-update vibe.
- API log/security complaint [10079] is highly idiosyncratic, log-dump style; not the same rhetorical cadence.
- Interview transcript [4642, 5623] not comparable.
- The coherence/representation theorem post [10154] is much more jokey/archaic register ("spake unto"), unlike query’s plain, sober tone.
- LLM model roundup [2468] is more newsletter-y/curatorial with lots of assertions; less self-critical model-updating and less historical analogy.

To find more by this author next hop: look for rationalist/EA/AI-safety community blog posts with explicit credences, talk of "models", "reference classes", postmortems/retrospectives, quantitative back-of-envelope comparisons, and pragmatic how-to/event-organizing posts using 80/20 framing and parenthetical asides.
hops.summary: Identified five candidates likely sharing the query author’s rationalist blog voice: first-person analytic posts with explicit uncertainty/credence framing, quantitative comparisons, and pragmatic explanatory structure. hops.search_query: "reference class" retrospective "I was overconfident" "measly" "Winter War" "for the record" credence "I gave"
hops.notes:
Strong matches share the query’s rationalist/EA-blogger fingerprint: first-person reflective postmortem framing ("what I hadn’t realized", "I no longer think it’s a slam dunk"), explicit epistemic status + numeric credences/confidence, and "model"/updating language. Several candidates have TL;DR but lack explicit self-critique/model-updating and feel like different subcultures (engineering-leadership pep talk, Claude-tooling notes, juggling guide).

hops.search_query: "It’s literally 5 lines of code" refusal-tuning "single activation direction" "universal refusal direction" "mode activations" karpathy 2015 "NeurIPS 2024 poster"
hops.notes:
Strong match signals: (1) didactic, mechanistic explanatory style with explicit causal framing (“It’s very simple, let me explain”, “failure mode”, “causal chain”), (2) heavy use of short paragraphs that step through an argument, (3) casual-but-precise register mixing informal hedges (“kinda”, “so …”) with technical terms (SFT, loss, A/B testing, Bayesian updating), (4) rhetorical scaffolding: setting up an example, then generalizing, then discussing testing/metrics failure modes, (5) occasional pseudo-code / math-probability language and meta-method discussion (“what tests check”, “overfitting”, “P(events|model)”), (6) punctuation habits: em-dashes, parentheses for asides, quotation marks for terms, colon lists.

Notable non-matches / missing patterns: Many candidates are polished magazine-style science journalism (Quanta/NYT tone), featuring narrative leads, quotes, and third-person reporting; they lack the author’s engineering/ML safety-tuning lens, lack direct second-person instructional voice, and rarely include code/math notations. Kernel/driver docs are technical but are formal spec prose without the bloggy rhetorical beats, informal asides, or safety/LLM policy framing.

Extra fingerprint to use next hop: blogosphere/EA-adjacent AI commentary; focuses on incentives, evaluation pitfalls, and how simple training hacks create degenerate shortcuts; uses concrete toy examples (sometimes code) to illustrate general alignment/product failure modes; pragmatic, slightly sardonic tone; frequent meta about tests/metrics and “what people don’t get”.
hops.summary: Found three candidates (10516, 5823, 2008) that share the query’s bloggy, mechanistic explanatory voice, incentive/testing focus, and probabilistic/ML-style reasoning. Most other texts are either formal kernel engineering prose or narrative science journalism and do not match stylistically.

Why top-scored items still don’t match: Several are AI-policy/blog commentary [3824, 8175, 10482] but are more polemical/manifesto-style, longer narrative arcs, less hands-on training mechanics, and no code. Extra fingerprints to use next hop: look for posts that (a) explain ML/alignment/product failures via incentive-compatible shortcuts/overfitting-to-metrics, (b) use toy constructions (“just insert token X into prompts”) and small snippets of Python-like pseudocode, (c) address evaluation design and how naive tests produce degenerate behaviors, (d) write in a casual, slightly sardonic, teach-by-example style with lots of short paragraphs and asides in parentheses.

hops.search_query: "Zero cost data" "cell-free DNA" universal non-invasive diagnostic "transplant samples" Quake lab
hops.notes:
Query text has a distinctive first-person scientific-narrative voice: autobiographical framing (“Much of my PhD work…”), clear chronological structure (1947 → 1990s → 2008), heavy use of technical biomedical vocabulary (cell-free DNA, plasma, NGS), quantitative specificity (~100 billion/ml; “up to 10%”), and an explicit argument scaffold with labeled section header and enumerated bullet reasons (“Fundamental / Zero cost data / Testable”). The tone is explanatory, research-contextual, and method/validation-oriented.

All candidates miss key fingerprints. Many are third-person magazine-style science journalism (Quanta-like) with scene-setting leads, quotes, and no first-person lab narrative ([2593], [5751], [4477], [11960], [3937], [6799], [9127], [3473])—wrong POV and structure. Others are informal internet/self-help/rant voice with slang, parentheticals, or strong affect ([6634], [10240], [11261], [3345], [4149])—wrong register. Several are ML/mech-interp technical posts but with different cadence: highly imperative, hackerish, or paper-abstract style; no biomed framing, no historical arc, no “why this problem” research-motivation bullets ([3172], [11128], [6440]). The DeSci piece ([4933]) is first-person but is rhetorical/philosophical, with snarky asides and no quantitative biomed exposition. None reproduce the combination of: (1) personal PhD origin story, (2) biomedical diagnostics context, (3) precise numeric claims, and (4) structured ‘Taste/Why’ + 3-part bullet justification.

To find more: look for posts with Markdown headers like “####”, a section explicitly motivating a research direction (“Why work on this problem?”), bullet lists with named categories, and biomedical/NGS/cell-free DNA/transplant/infectious disease terminology, plus a calm explanatory tone and frequent numeric back-of-envelope estimates.
hops.summary: No candidate text appears to be by the same author as the query; closest topical adjacency is a COVID eradication explainer ([3972]) but it is third-person and lacks the query’s first-person PhD narrative and structured motivation bullets.

hops.search_query: "####Taste" "Why work on this" "Zero cost data" "Testable" cell-free DNA NGS transplant rejection
hops.notes:
Best match is [244]. It shares multiple distinctive fingerprints from the query: (1) explicit focus on “research taste” with an almost identical framing; the query even has a “####Taste: Why work on this problem?” header, and [244] opens by defining research taste and motivating it. (2) First-person reflective voice with hedges and humility (“I wanted to share…”, “grain of salt”, “I’m hardly an expert”), similar to the query’s autobiographical lab-narrative stance. (3) Clear pedagogical structuring with Markdown-like sectioning and enumerated items; the query uses a labeled header and a 3-part named bullet rationale (“Fundamental / Zero cost data / Testable”), while [244] uses “Exercises” + numbered exercises with brief justifications. (4) Sentence cadence: short, direct claims followed by explanatory expansions and parenthetical asides.

All other candidates strongly mismatch the authorial profile: many are third-person science journalism with quotations and scene-setting ledes ([5153], [11860], [7452], [4051], [9793], [6894], [6948], [10514], [2971], [5540], [3980]) and thus lack first-person research autobiography + argument scaffolding. Several are highly technical but in an impersonal, theorem/abstract/manual style without the taste/motivation framing ([7246], [969], [8004], [7067], [5657]). Others are EA/AI-safety program promos or policy commentary with organizational voice or snarky rhetoric ([10972], [3309], [9989])—different tone and rhetorical habits.

To find more by this author next hop: search for posts that explicitly discuss “research taste” or “why this problem”, use Markdown headers (often ‘####’), and present structured rationales with named bullet categories or numbered lists. Expect first-person mentorship/managerial references (“people I mentored or managed”), pragmatic advice, and a calm explanatory tone with occasional typos (e.g., “chose”, “think”, “twiter”, “resarch”). Also look for content spanning computational biology/NGS/cell-free DNA alongside meta-research/career advice—same author may write both technical bio posts and research-process posts.
hops.summary: Exactly one strong same-author hit: [244], which matches the query’s rare combination of first-person research narrative plus explicit ‘research taste’ framing and structured list-based argumentation. The rest are predominantly third-person journalism or mismatched technical/promo styles.
